column2: On the authority of Muʿādh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I said: “O Messenger of Allah, tell me of a deed that will admit me to Paradise and keep me far from the Fire.” He said:

“You have asked about something great, yet it is easy for the one for whom Allah the Exalted makes it easy: worship Allah without associating anything with Him, establish the prayer, give the zakāh, fast Ramaḍān

and make pilgrimage to the House.” Then he said: “Shall I not guide you to the gates of good? Fasting is a shield; charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire; and a man's prayer in the depth of the night.”

Then he recited: “Their sides forsake their beds…” until he reached “…they used to do” [al-Sajdah 32:16–17]. Then he said: “Shall I not tell you of the head of the matter, its pillar and its highest peak?
…jihād.” Then he said: “Shall I not tell you of what holds all of that together?”
I said: “Yes indeed, O Messenger of Allah.” He took hold of his tongue and said: “Restrain this.”
I said: “O Prophet of Allah, will we really be taken to account for what we say?”

He said: “May your mother be bereaved of you! Is there anything that topples people into the Fire on their faces”—or he said: “on their noses—except the harvests of their tongues?” Reported by al-Tirmidhī, who said: A ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith.

The edition omits part of the hadith before «الجهاد»: Muʿādh's reply and the words «رأس الأمر الإسلام وعموده الصلاة وذروة سنامه» (“The head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer, and its highest peak is…”). The translation follows the printed text and marks the gap with an ellipsis.

“You have asked about something great”: about a great deed, because entering Paradise and being saved from the Fire is an extremely great matter, for whose sake Allah sent down the books and sent the messengers.
“For whom Allah makes it easy”: by enabling him to carry out acts of obedience as they should be done.
Taʿbudu Allāh (“worship Allah”): affirm His oneness.
“To the gates of good”: of voluntary deeds, since he had already directed him to the obligations of Islam.
Al-ṣawm (“fasting”): doing much of the voluntary fast, since the obligatory fast was mentioned just before.
Junnah (“a shield”): with ḍammah on the jīm; a protection for the one who fasts from sins in this world and from the Fire in the Hereafter.
Al-ṣadaqah (“charity”): voluntary charity, since the obligatory one was mentioned before.

“And a man's prayer in the depth of the night”: meaning that it extinguishes sin. A woman is like a man in this; the man is mentioned specifically only because good predominates among men, or because the questioner was a man.
Talā (“he recited”): the Prophet ﷺ recited, to make clear the virtue of the night prayer.
Tatajāfā (“forsake”): move away from.
Al-maḍājiʿ (“their beds”): the places where one lies down to sleep.
“Then he said”: the Prophet ﷺ said.
“Of the head of the matter”: which you asked about.
Dhurwah (“highest peak”): with ḍammah or kasrah on the dhāl; the topmost part.
“Of what holds all of that together (bi-milāki dhālika kullih)”: its essence and what gathers it, on which it relies.
Milāk is with kasrah or fatḥah on the mīm.
“He took hold of his tongue”: the Prophet ﷺ took hold of his own tongue.
“Restrain this (kuff ʿalayka)”: [restrain] from yourself;
or kuff carries the sense of “confine”.
Thakilatka (“may [your mother] be bereaved of you”): may she lose you. The Messenger of Allah did not intend the literal supplication;
rather, it follows the custom of the Arabs in their ways of addressing one another.
Wa-hal (“is there anything…”): a rhetorical question of denial, in the sense of negation.
Yakubbu (“topples”): with ḍammah on the kāf; throws down.
Al-nās (“people”): most of them.
“The harvests of their tongues”: the speech they reap that has no good in it.
Muʿādh's (may Allah be pleased with him) intense concern for righteous deeds.

Righteous deeds are a cause of entering Paradise, as the Exalted said: “And that is Paradise, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do” [al-Zukhruf 43:72]. As for his ﷺ saying, “None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds”,

what is meant is that by the deed itself no one deserves Paradise, were it not that Allah, by His favour and mercy, has made it a cause of that; and the deed itself is from Allah's favour and mercy to His servant. So Paradise and its causes are all from Allah's favour and mercy.
Success is in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: whoever has guidance made easy for him is guided,
and whoever does not have it made easy for him, it is not made easy.
Entering Paradise depends on doing the five pillars of Islam: tawḥīd, prayer, zakāh, fasting and Ḥajj.
The virtue of drawing near [to Allah] through voluntary deeds after performing the obligations.
Bad deeds are expiated by charity.
The virtue of praying in the depth of the night.
The prayer is to Islam as the pole on which a tent stands: Islam goes when it goes, just as the tent falls when its pole falls.
The virtue of jihād.
Restraining, controlling and confining the tongue is the root of all good; for the sin of speech includes shirk, which is the greatest of sins with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic;
speaking about Allah without knowledge, which is the companion of shirk; false testimony; sorcery; slander; backbiting; talebearing; and all the other sins of speech.
Indeed, the sins of action are generally not free of words that accompany them and help to bring them about.
